title: Code-Switching in the Body
hook: Many men walk into work as a slightly different body from the one that walked out of the house, and the switch costs more than anyone sees.
why:
Most men adjust their bodies between settings. The greeting with old friends becomes a handshake at work. The laugh gets quieter, the accent shifts, the hands stay still, the posture straightens. For some men these are small adjustments, made without thought. For others, especially men whose race, class, faith, sexuality, accent or background differs from the people who set the rules of the room, the adjustment is larger, constant and tiring.

Earlier chapters in this part described several of these situations one at a time: masking, class codes, the way Black men's bodies are read, the queer dialect, the codes of faith. This chapter looks at what they have in common: the act of switching itself, what it costs, when it is a skill and when it is a burden, and how to read other men's switches without exposing or judging them.

The aim is not to stop switching. Everyone adapts to context, and some adaptation is courtesy. The aim is to see the switch clearly, in yourself and in others, and to make rooms in which fewer people have to work so hard to belong.

teach.p:
The term code-switching comes from linguistics, where it describes people who move between languages or dialects depending on whom they are talking to. It has come to describe something broader: the way people adjust their speech, appearance, behaviour and expression to fit the norms of different settings, especially when their own group is not the one that set those norms.

Much of code-switching happens in the body. A man may greet his friends with a slap of hands, a pull into a hug and a loud laugh, and greet his colleagues with a measured handshake and a nod. He may sit back and spread out at home and sit upright and contained in meetings. He may gesture freely with family and keep his hands still at work. His voice may drop in pitch and lose its regional edge when he picks up the office phone.

Everyone does some of this. The psychologist Mark Snyder described a trait he called self-monitoring: the degree to which people watch social situations and adjust their behaviour to fit. High self-monitors switch readily and often well. But the size of the switch varies enormously, depending on how far a man's home codes are from the codes of the rooms where he works and is judged.

The figures here greet each other with a fist bump, the kind of greeting that might be second nature with friends and swapped for a handshake as soon as a manager walks in. Neither greeting is the real one. Both are his.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people behaved the same way across settings. Research on self-monitoring and on code-switching shows that most people adjust their behaviour to context, and that the size of the adjustment varies with the distance between their codes and the room's.

teach.p:
In 2019 Courtney McCluney, Kathrina Robotham, Serenity Lee, Richard Smith and Myles Durkee summarised research on how Black employees in the United States code-switch at work: adjusting speech, appearance and behaviour, and avoiding topics or habits associated with negative stereotypes, in order to be seen as professional and to be treated fairly.

A later experiment by McCluney and colleagues, published in 2021, tested how that switching is read. Participants evaluated a fictional Black employee whose speech style, name and hairstyle either conformed to white professional norms or did not. Both Black and white participants rated the employee who code-switched as more professional. The finding confirms what many Black men already know: switching is rewarded. It also shows why switching continues even when it costs the switcher.

The costs are the other half of the picture. People who describe frequent code-switching report fatigue, a sense of being watched, and the strain of keeping part of themselves out of sight. The authors argued that organisations should widen what counts as professional, rather than leaving the work of fitting in to the people who differ most from the norm.

The figure here stands tall and at ease, hands loose, face neutral. What the picture cannot show is how much of that ease has been built for the room, and how much it costs to hold it all day.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if code-switching made no difference to how Black employees were judged. McCluney and colleagues found that both Black and white observers rated code-switching employees as more professional.
teach.pullQuote: Switching is rewarded, which is why it continues even when it costs the switcher.

teach.p:
In 2006 the legal scholar Kenji Yoshino described a related idea, which he called covering. Borrowing a term from the sociologist Erving Goffman, he distinguished it from passing. A man who passes hides an identity entirely. A man who covers lets the identity be known but plays it down so that it does not make others uncomfortable.

Yoshino identified four ways people cover. They change their appearance: hair, dress, grooming, the way they move. They limit their affiliation: avoiding behaviour associated with their group, such as an accent or certain foods. They hold back on advocacy: not speaking up for their group. And they manage association: avoiding being seen with other members of their group.

In 2013 Yoshino and Christie Smith of Deloitte surveyed employees in large American companies about covering. A majority said they covered in at least one of these ways, and so did about half of straight white men, who described covering things such as mental health conditions, religion, age or family responsibilities. Many said that covering harmed their sense of themselves.

Covering often shows in the body: a man who never mentions his children because he fears looking less committed, who hides a limp, who turns his prayer beads into his pocket when the door opens, who laughs along at jokes about his own background. The figure here stands upright and braced, the posture of a man holding part of himself in check.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if covering were rare or limited to minority groups. Yoshino and Smith's survey found that a majority of employees covered, including about half of straight white men.

teach.p:
In 2007 Andrew Molinsky described what happens when people must adapt their behaviour to a foreign culture, such as a manager from a reserved culture who must promote himself in an American job interview, or an American posted to Japan who must learn to disagree indirectly. He called it cross-cultural code-switching, and identified two kinds of difficulty.

The first is competence: performing an unfamiliar behaviour well. A man raised to downplay his achievements may simply not know how to describe them with the confidence an American interviewer expects, and his attempt may come out stiff or overdone. The second is identity: performing a behaviour that conflicts with his values. Self-promotion may feel boastful and wrong, even when he knows it is expected. Both difficulties can produce anxiety, embarrassment and resentment, and both show in the body as hesitation, mismatched expressions or overcorrection.

Molinsky's later work, on what he called global dexterity, suggested that people adapt more comfortably when they find a version of the new behaviour they can live with: a way of describing achievements that feels like reporting facts rather than boasting, a way of disagreeing that feels like helping.

The figure here presents to a room, open and confident. For some men this comes naturally; for others it is a foreign language spoken with an accent of discomfort that the audience may misread as weakness.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if adapting to a foreign cultural code were simply a matter of learning the rules. Molinsky's work shows that the psychological challenges of competence and identity make the switch difficult even for people who know what is expected.

teach.p:
In 1983 the sociologist Arlie Hochschild introduced the idea of emotional labour: the work of managing feelings and their expression as part of a job. She distinguished surface acting, in which a person displays an emotion he does not feel, such as a smile over irritation, from deep acting, in which he tries to actually feel the emotion he needs to display.

In 2011 Ute Hülsheger and Anna Schewe combined ninety-five studies of emotional labour. Surface acting was strongly linked to poorer well-being, including exhaustion, and to worse job attitudes. Deep acting had only weak links to poor well-being and was linked to better performance. Showing what you do not feel, all day, appears to be the costly part.

A popular explanation for this kind of fatigue was ego depletion: the idea that self-control draws on a limited store of willpower that runs down with use. When twenty-three laboratories tried to reproduce a standard ego-depletion effect in 2016, the pooled effect was close to zero. So it is better not to explain the cost of switching as an emptying tank. A more careful account is that constant monitoring, of yourself and of how you are being read, is effortful, and that hiding what you feel conflicts with your sense of who you are.

The figure here slumps after a video call, the posture of the moment the performance ends. For many men, that moment is the first time all day the body says what it feels.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if displaying unfelt emotions had no link to well-being. Hülsheger and Schewe found that surface acting was consistently associated with exhaustion and poorer well-being across ninety-five studies.

teach.p:
Switching has real benefits. A 2002 meta-analysis by David Day and colleagues found that high self-monitors, the people who most readily adapt their behaviour to the situation, tended to receive better performance ratings and to emerge more often as leaders. The ability to read a room and fit it is a skill, and many men who code-switch fluently are proud of it.

The difference between skill and survival lies in choice and cost. A man who switches because he wants to, in a way he endorses, and who can drop the switch when he goes home, is using a skill. A man who switches because he fears being judged, punished or harmed if he does not, and who cannot drop it even in safe company, is surviving. The same behaviour can be either.

A few signs suggest the switch is costing more than it should: exhaustion after days that were not otherwise demanding; a sense of being an impostor in both worlds; irritability at home; difficulty knowing which version of yourself is the real one; relief, out of proportion, when you are among people who share your background.

The figure here exhales, shoulders dropping, the breath of a man letting go of a held posture. Noticing when and where that breath comes is one way to learn where you have been switching hardest.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if adapting to context were always costly. Day and colleagues found that high self-monitors tend to be rated as better performers and to emerge as leaders, so switching can be a genuine skill.

teach.p:
For a reader of other men, code-switching raises a few practical rules. The first is not to call it out. Remarking that a colleague sounds different on the phone to his mother, or that he has gone quiet now that the boss is here, exposes a switch he may have worked hard to make invisible.

The second is not to rank the selves. It is tempting to treat the home self as the authentic one and the work self as a mask, or the reverse. Both are real. A man who speaks differently with his grandmother and with his clients is not lying to either of them.

The third is to look at the room rather than the man. If many people in a team are switching hard, the team's norms are probably narrower than the work requires. Leaders can widen them: by not policing accents, hair or dress beyond genuine need; by sharing something of their own life; by making it normal to mention children, faith, illness or background; by noticing who seems most relaxed and who seems most braced.

And the fourth is to offer, where you can, a room where the switch is not needed. The figures here walk side by side, at ease. Many men describe the friend or colleague with whom they do not have to switch at all as one of the most valuable people in their lives.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if remarking on someone's switch were harmless. People who code-switch describe being called out on it as exposing and embarrassing, because it draws attention to the very difference they are managing.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting it ease where it is safe
poseGallery.dontCaption: Holding the work posture all day
poseGallery.annotation: Notice where you are bracing, and find the places where you can let the posture drop.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Pointing out a colleague's switch in front of others
poseGallery.annotation: A switch is often hard work. Do not expose it; make the room easier instead.

poseGallery.doCaption: Building small releases into the day
poseGallery.dontCaption: Collapsing only when the camera goes off
poseGallery.annotation: If the only release comes at the end of the day, the day is costing too much. Build in a few breaths of ease.

poseGallery.doCaption: At ease, back to the room, at home
poseGallery.dontCaption: Still braced and scanning at the family table
poseGallery.annotation: A work body that will not switch off is common after long periods of vigilance. Small release points help it learn that home is safe.

poseGallery.doCaption: Talking as equals about his daughter
poseGallery.dontCaption: Stiff and formal at a school meeting
poseGallery.annotation: Switching to be taken seriously can crowd out the conversation. An open question gives the person room.

caseStudy:
Marcus, thirty-six, is a solicitor in a London firm. He grew up on an estate in south London, the son of Jamaican parents, and was the first in his family to go to university. At work he speaks in the even, unaccented English his colleagues use, keeps his hair cut short, wears the same navy suits as everyone else and laughs politely at jokes about places he has never been. At his mother's house on Sundays, his voice changes before he has taken his coat off.

For years he thought of this as a skill, and in many ways it was. He won clients, impressed partners and was promoted early. But by his mid-thirties he noticed that he was exhausted on Friday nights in a way the work did not explain, and that he was short with his son when he got home.

The turning point came at a team lunch. A colleague, overhearing him on the phone to his brother, imitated his accent and said that he had not known Marcus could talk like that. Everyone laughed. Marcus laughed too, and then sat in the toilet for ten minutes with his heart racing.

He told a senior partner, Ruth, what had happened. Ruth spoke to the colleague privately, and then did something Marcus had not expected: she began to talk at team meetings about her own background in a northern mining town, and to make it normal for people to mention where they came from.

Marcus still switches. But he has found a few places where he does not have to, including Ruth's office, and he says the Friday exhaustion is less than it was.
observe: Notice the moments in your day when your posture, voice or gestures change, and what triggers each change.
Notice where you feel most at ease and least watched, and what is different about those places.
Notice colleagues who seem most braced at work, and what the room might be asking of them.
Notice any urge to comment on someone's switch, and what saying it aloud would do to them.

drills.name: Switch Map
steps: Draw a simple map of your week: home, work, friends, family, any other regular settings.
For each, note how your voice, posture, gestures and greetings differ.
Mark which switches you choose freely and which you make because you feel you must.
Mark which switches leave you most tired.
Choose one costly switch to look at more closely.
variations: Add online spaces to your map, such as work chats, family groups and social media, and note how you switch in each.
Ask someone who sees you in two settings, such as a partner or an old friend, how differently you come across in each.
Mark the switches that you are proud of as well as the ones that cost you, since not all switching is a burden.

drills.name: Release Points
steps: Notice, over one working day, the moments when your body relaxes: an exhale, shoulders dropping, a change of voice.
Write down when and where each happened.
Ask what the release tells you about the hours before it.
Plan two small releases into tomorrow, such as a walk or a call with a friend.
variations: Try a release point at the moment you notice tension building, rather than waiting until the end of the day.
Notice whether your release points involve particular people, places or activities, and plan more of the ones that work.
On a day with no release points, notice how you feel by the evening, and what you would change.

drills.name: Widen the Room
steps: If you lead a team or a group, list the unwritten norms of dress, speech and behaviour in it.
Mark which are needed for the work and which are habit.
Choose one habit-norm to relax, such as by sharing something about your own background.
Notice over the following weeks who seems more at ease.
variations: Ask a colleague from a different background which of your team's norms they find hardest, and listen without defending them.
Relax one norm for a trial month, such as a dress expectation, and ask people afterwards whether it made a difference.
Notice which jokes in your team are about where people come from, and whether everyone laughs.

drills.name: The Unswitched Friend
steps: Think of a person with whom you do not have to switch at all.
Arrange to spend time with them this week.
Notice how your body feels in their company compared with at work.
Write a few lines about what that difference tells you.
variations: Notice your posture, voice and breathing in the first five minutes with the unswitched friend, and compare them with the first five minutes at work.
If you cannot think of anyone with whom you do not switch, notice that, and consider who might become that person.
Tell the friend, if it feels right, that time with them is one of the few places you can stop switching.

quiz.q: A colleague says that a man who talks and moves differently with his friends than with clients is being fake. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since the self a man shows at home is the only real one, and the rest is an act
Adjusting to different settings is common and often skilled, and both versions can be real
He is right, since the self a man shows at work is the only real one, and the rest is an act
Men should behave in exactly the same way everywhere, so that they are never seen as fake
quiz.explain: Most people adapt their behaviour to context, and high self-monitors do so readily. A man who speaks differently with his grandmother and his clients is not lying to either.

quiz.q: What did McCluney and colleagues find in their 2021 experiment on racial code-switching?
options: Both Black and white participants rated the code-switching employee as more professional
Only white participants noticed code-switching, and they rated it as less professional
Code-switching made no difference to how professional the employee was judged to be
Black participants rated the code-switching employee as less professional than others did
quiz.explain: Both groups rated the employee who conformed to white professional norms as more professional. That reward is part of why switching continues even when it is costly.

quiz.q: What did Yoshino and Smith's 2013 survey find about covering at work?
options: Only members of minority groups reported covering any part of their identity at work
Almost no employees covered, because large companies had already removed the need
A majority covered in some way, including about half of straight white men surveyed
Covering was common but was found to improve commitment to the organisation overall
quiz.explain: Covering was widespread, and not only among minorities. Straight white men covered things such as mental health, religion and family background.

quiz.q: What did Hülsheger and Schewe's 2011 meta-analysis find about emotional labour?
options: Deep acting, trying to feel the required emotion, was the main cause of exhaustion
Neither surface nor deep acting had any link to well-being in the studies reviewed
Surface acting was linked to better performance and well-being than deep acting
Surface acting, showing emotions not felt, was linked to exhaustion and poor well-being
quiz.explain: Across ninety-five studies, surface acting was associated with poorer well-being, including exhaustion. Deep acting had only weak links to poor well-being and was linked to better performance.

quiz.q: At a team lunch, a colleague hears another man speaking in a strong regional accent on the phone to his brother, and starts imitating it. What fits this chapter best?
options: Join in the joke, since it is light-hearted and shows that the team is relaxed together
Do not join in, and later tell the colleague privately that this is not something to mock
Ask the man in front of everyone why he does not speak like that at work all the time
Say nothing at all, since how people speak is entirely their own private business
quiz.explain: Calling out someone's switch exposes the difference he is managing. Declining to join in, and addressing it privately, protects him without adding to the embarrassment.

quiz.q: You notice you are exhausted after client days, though the work itself is not hard, and you are short with your family when you get home. What fits this chapter best?
options: Push through it, since tiredness after work is simply the price of a career
Stop adapting to clients altogether, since adapting to them is always a mistake
Notice which switches cost most, and build in places where you can drop them
Assume your willpower is running out, and rest until it has been fully restored
quiz.explain: The pattern fits a costly switch. Mapping which adaptations cost most, and making room to drop them, addresses the cause; the willpower-tank account is not well supported.

quiz.q: What did Day and colleagues' 2002 meta-analysis find about high self-monitors, people who readily adapt their behaviour to the situation?
options: That they were rated as less trustworthy and less effective than other employees
That they tended to receive better performance ratings and to emerge as leaders
That they were more likely to leave their jobs within a year of starting them
That they showed no difference at all from other people in how they were rated
quiz.explain: High self-monitors tended to receive better performance ratings and to emerge more often as leaders. Switching is a real skill; the problem is its cost when it is constant and unchosen.

quiz.q: At a parents' evening, a father sits stiffly, speaks in a careful, formal voice, nods often and asks no questions. What fits this chapter best?
options: Conclude that he is not very engaged with his child's education
Consider that he may be switching to be taken seriously, and ask an open question
Tell him he can relax and speak however he likes, since it is only a parents' evening
Mention his manner to the form tutor, so that the school knows the family is distant
quiz.explain: Many men switch in exactly the institutions that matter most for their families, and the effort can crowd out the conversation itself. An open question and a pause give him room without exposing the switch.

quiz.q: Someone says that code-switching is tiring because willpower is a limited tank that runs out over the day. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That the willpower-tank idea has not held up, and the effort of monitoring and hiding is the likelier cause
That the willpower-tank idea has been fully confirmed by every large study that has tested it carefully
That code-switching is not tiring at all once a person has practised it for a few years at work
That only people who are bad at switching find it tiring, since skilled switchers feel nothing at all
quiz.explain: The popular explanation of ego depletion has not held up in large replications. The ongoing effort of monitoring yourself and the strain of hiding parts of who you are are the more likely sources of the fatigue.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific setting in which you switch: a workplace, a family, a group of friends, a place of worship. Describe what changes in your body when you enter it: voice, posture, gestures, laughter, greeting. Is the switch something you choose, or something you feel you must do? What does it cost you, and what does it give you? Then think of one place where you do not switch at all, and what makes it different.
reflection.guidance: This can be a tender subject, especially for men who have moved a long way from where they started. Write about specific behaviours rather than about which self is real. Both are yours. If you lead others, consider also what your rooms ask of the people in them.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat one version of a man as real and the other as fake, when both are his. The second is to call out a switch in public, exposing the difference he is managing. The third is to assume switching is free: to miss the fatigue, vigilance and identity strain that constant switching can carry. The fourth is to explain that cost with the discredited idea of a willpower tank, rather than the effort of monitoring and the strain of hiding. The fifth, for leaders, is to keep norms narrower than the work requires, so that the people who differ most from the norm work hardest to fit. And the sixth, for oneself, is to never notice where the switch has become survival rather than skill.

moreCases.title: The engineer who would not sell himself
moreCases.scene:
Piotr, forty-one, is a civil engineer who moved to Britain from Poland twelve years ago. He leads a team of eight on a large bridge project, and
  his work is known across the firm for being meticulous. He is applying for promotion to associate director, and the final stage is a panel interview
  with three directors.

  In the interview, he is asked to describe his biggest achievement. He talks about the bridge project, but mostly in terms of the team: "We managed to
  solve the foundation problem," "The team worked very hard." When asked what he personally contributed, he says, "I coordinated," and stops. When asked
  where he sees himself in five years, he says he hopes to be useful to the firm. He sits very still, hands folded, and smiles little.

  The panel is split. One director writes that Piotr "lacks confidence and leadership presence". Another notes that he "undersells himself". The third,
  Alison, who has worked with engineers from many countries, says that she suspects they are hearing a cultural habit of modesty rather than a lack
  of achievement, and suggests they look at the project record.

  The record shows that Piotr designed the solution to the foundation problem himself, over a weekend, and saved the client four months. He had not
  thought it appropriate to say so.

Afterwards, he tells his wife that the interview went badly because they asked him to talk about himself, which he finds embarrassing in any language.

His previous manager had once told him, kindly, that in Britain you had to "blow your own trumpet a bit". Piotr had nodded, and had not known how.

His team, when they hear later that he was nearly turned down for lacking leadership, are baffled. Several of them say that he is the best leader they have had, precisely because he never takes the credit.
moreCases.misread:
Two of the panel read Piotr's modest account, his use of "we" and his stillness as a lack of confidence and leadership. Piotr read the interview's invitation to boast as something to be handled with restraint, as he had been taught, and assumed his record would speak for him.

The director who wrote "lacks presence" also read Piotr's stillness as nerves, when it was the composure of a man who did not think it polite to fidget in front of senior people.

He also read the panel's silence after his answers as satisfaction, because in his experience a modest answer was received well, and did not realise until afterwards that they had been waiting for more.

The third director, Alison, read the same answers through her experience of colleagues from many countries, which is why she asked to see the record before deciding.
moreCases.betterRead:
Molinsky described cross-cultural code-switching as carrying two difficulties: competence, knowing how to perform an unfamiliar behaviour, and identity, performing one that conflicts with your values. For Piotr, self-promotion was both unfamiliar and, in his upbringing, close to bad manners. His modesty was a norm, not a deficit. The better reading, which Alison prompted, was to judge the evidence of what he had done, as structured assessments are meant to. The panel promoted him. Alison also offered, afterwards, to talk with Piotr about how the firm's directors expected people to describe their work, framing it as a local custom rather than a correction. Piotr decided to adapt partly: he now describes his own contribution plainly when asked, and still credits his team first, which he says is the version of himself he can live with.

Alison also suggested that the firm's interview guidance mention that modesty about achievements varies between cultures, so that future panels would check the record before reading reticence as weakness.

He also began mentoring two junior engineers from abroad, explaining the unwritten rules he had learned the hard way.

moreCases.title: The teacher who covered
moreCases.scene:
Jamie, thirty-one, teaches English at a secondary school, and he is gay. He is out to the staff, and nobody has ever said anything unkind. But he
  has never mentioned his partner, Tom, at work, never put a photograph on his desk, and always says "we" vaguely when asked about his weekend. He
  dresses more plainly than he does at home, keeps his gestures smaller in front of classes and has declined, twice, to help run the school's LGBT
  group. He tells himself that this is just professionalism.

  At the end of a hard term, he is exhausted in a way that the marking does not explain. He realises that he has spent every day editing himself: what
  he says, how he moves, which stories he tells. A colleague, Hannah, mentions her husband several times a day without thinking about it. Jamie has
  mentioned Tom perhaps twice in three years.

  At the staff Christmas party, a colleague asks him, in front of others, whether he is "still single". Jamie hesitates, then says, "No, I've been with
  Tom for six years." There is a short pause. Then the colleague says, "Oh, brilliant, bring him next time," and moves on.

  On the way home, Jamie notices that his shoulders have dropped for the first time in months.

He also realises that he has never told his students he is gay, which is his choice, and that he has also never told the colleague he shares a classroom with, which is a choice he is no longer sure he made.

He also realises that he had chosen his school partly because he thought he would not need to cover there, and that he had covered anyway, out of habit.

Hannah, who mentions her husband constantly, has no idea that she has been the measure of something for Jamie. When he tells her later, she is quiet for a moment and then says she wishes she had asked about his weekends properly.
moreCases.misread:
Jamie read his own editing as ordinary professionalism and did not notice how much of the working day it consumed. His colleagues, for their part, read his vagueness about weekends as privacy, and had no idea of the effort behind it.

The colleague who asked whether he was still single read Jamie's vagueness over the years as having nothing to share, and was delighted to be told otherwise.

He also read the brief pause at the party as the beginning of the judgment he had always feared, when it was simply a colleague catching up with news she had never been given.
moreCases.betterRead:
Yoshino described covering: letting an identity be known but playing it down so that it does not make others uncomfortable, by changing appearance, limiting affiliation, holding back on advocacy and managing association. Yoshino and Smith's survey found covering common across large companies, and this chapter describes how much of it happens in the body. Jamie was covering on several of those dimensions at once, and the effort showed as exhaustion. The better path, which began at the party, was his own to choose: to let go of the covering that cost most and protected least. He put a photograph of Tom on his desk in January. The following year he agreed to help run the LGBT group. The head teacher, hearing about it, made a point of using neutral language in staff communications and mentioning partners of all kinds in the staff newsletter. Jamie still chooses what to share, as everyone does. He no longer edits every sentence.

He also noticed that two students in his form, months later, told him about their own families more openly than before, though he never knew whether the photograph had anything to do with it.

moreCases.title: The father at parents' evening
moreCases.scene:
Delroy, forty-five, is a bus driver, a Black British man who grew up in Birmingham and speaks, with his friends and family, in a warm, expressive
  mix of Brummie and Jamaican English. At his daughter Keisha's parents' evening, he arrives in a pressed shirt, sits very upright in the small plastic
  chair, folds his hands on the table and speaks in what his wife calls his telephone voice: slow, careful and flattened, with every consonant in place.

  The teacher, Mr Hodges, explains that Keisha's work has slipped this term and asks whether there is anything going on at home. Delroy answers in
  short, formal sentences: "Not that I'm aware of." "We'll speak to her." "Thank you for letting us know." He nods often and does not ask any questions.

  Mr Hodges comes away with the impression of a father who is not very engaged with his daughter's education. He mentions to Keisha's form tutor that
  the parents did not seem particularly concerned.

  In the car park, Delroy's wife asks him why he went so stiff. He says that he always does, in schools and hospitals and banks, because he has learned
  that if he talks like himself, people decide he is aggressive or stupid before he has finished a sentence. He says that he was so busy talking
  properly that he forgot to ask about the maths.

Keisha, who has come with them, notices the change in her father's voice as soon as he sits down, and tells her mother later that she hates it when he does that, because it makes him sound like a stranger.

At home that evening, he tells Keisha about the maths, in his own voice, and she explains what has been going wrong, which she had not told anyone at school.

Mr Hodges, it turns out, had seen eighteen sets of parents that evening, and Delroy and his wife were the seventeenth. He was tired, and had read the stiffness quickly.

Delroy also remembers his own father at parents' evenings in the 1980s, saying almost nothing, and his teachers writing on his report that his parents seemed uninterested. He had resolved to be different, and then found himself doing the same thing for the same reason.
moreCases.misread:
Mr Hodges read Delroy's stiffness, formal speech and lack of questions as disengagement from his daughter's education. Delroy's careful switch, made to be taken seriously, had used up the attention he needed for the conversation itself.

The form tutor, hearing Mr Hodges's account, read it as one more sign that the family was distant, which might have followed Keisha through the rest of the year.

Delroy, for his part, read Mr Hodges's brisk manner as confirmation that he was being judged, which made his voice more careful still.

And Keisha read her father's telephone voice as a stranger's, which is one of the costs of switching that falls on the people who know the switcher best.
moreCases.betterRead:
McCluney and colleagues found that Black employees who code-switched were rated as more professional, and summarised research on how such switching is used to avoid negative stereotypes. Outside work, many Black men switch in exactly the institutions that matter most for their families: schools, hospitals, banks and offices. The cost here was attention. Delroy's switch was so effortful that it crowded out the questions he wanted to ask, and the result was read as indifference. The better reading would have looked past the formality to what the father was doing: coming, in a pressed shirt, after a shift, to talk about his daughter. Mr Hodges might have asked an open question, such as "What would be useful for you to know?", and waited. Delroy rang the school the next day and asked about the maths. Mr Hodges, hearing his ordinary voice on the phone, noticed the difference, and thought about it.

Mr Hodges also began starting every parents' evening conversation by asking what the parents would like to know, before giving his own view, and found the meetings went better with everyone.

moreCases.title: The soldier home on leave
moreCases.scene:
Connor, twenty-seven, is a corporal in the army, home on leave for two weeks after a six-month deployment. At work, for six months, his body has
  been doing what it was trained to do: upright, alert, scanning every room, back to a wall, voice clipped and loud, sleep light, every movement
  efficient. He is very good at his job.

  At home, the switch does not come back. At his sister's birthday meal in a crowded restaurant, he takes the seat facing the door, sits braced and
  upright throughout, scans the room every few minutes and answers questions in short, clipped sentences. When a tray of glasses crashes in the
  kitchen, he is half out of his seat before he has thought. His nephew, eight, asks him why he is so serious. His girlfriend, Becca, finds him
  distant and hard to reach, and wonders whether something has changed between them.

  On the third night, Becca asks him, carefully, whether he is all right. Connor says he is fine. Then he says that he does not know how to stop being
  at work.

  His father, who served twenty years earlier, overhears and sits down with him on the back step.

Earlier that day, in the supermarket, he had found himself moving through the aisles as if clearing a building, and had laughed at himself, and then not laughed.

At home, he also notices that he makes his bed with hospital corners every morning and lays out his clothes for the next day, as if for inspection, and that his mother watches him do it.

His nephew also asks why Uncle Connor will not sit with his back to the window, and Connor, to his own surprise, cannot answer.
moreCases.misread:
Becca read Connor's braced, scanning, clipped manner as distance from her, and wondered whether the relationship had changed. His nephew read it as seriousness. Connor read his own failure to switch off as a fault in himself.

His sister read his clipped answers as irritation at being there, and nearly cried in the toilets halfway through her own birthday meal.

Connor also read Becca's question as a sign that she had noticed something wrong with him, which made him more guarded for a moment before he answered honestly.

Becca's friends, when she mentions it, suggest that he might have met someone else while away, which is a reading of distance that had nothing to do with the cause.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter describes the difference between switching as a skill, chosen and droppable, and switching as survival, which cannot be dropped even in safe company. Connor's work body was a skill that months of deployment had made automatic, and it had not yet learned that the restaurant was safe. His father's better response came from experience: he told Connor that it had taken him weeks to stop sitting facing the door, that it was normal, and that it would ease with time. He suggested small release points: a long walk every morning, an evening with one old friend rather than a crowd, and sitting with his back to the room once, on purpose, to see how it felt. Becca learned not to take the distance personally. When the alertness had not eased by the end of his leave, Connor spoke to his unit's welfare officer, who arranged support. He told Becca that knowing it was common helped more than anything else.

His father also told him, that night on the step, that he still sometimes sat facing the door in restaurants, thirty years on, and that it no longer bothered him.

workedReading.title: Widening the room as a team leader
workedReading.scene:
Bev, fifty-two, is head of planning at a city council, with a team of eighteen. Over her first year she has noticed something she finds hard to name. Several of her newer staff, the ones from backgrounds unlike the senior planners', seem braced at work in a way the others do not: very formal in meetings, careful about what they wear and say, quiet at the team social, and noticeably more relaxed when she bumps into them outside work. One, Kwame, a talented young planner, told her in his exit interview from a previous job, which he showed her, that he had left because he was tired of being someone else all day. Bev does not want to lose people for that reason. She decides to use the Widen the Room drill in this chapter, starting by looking at the norms rather than at the people.

She also knows that she switches herself, more than anyone in the department realises: her Lincolnshire voice has been sanded smooth over thirty years of committee meetings, and it comes back only when she is tired or with her sister.

She also suspects that the newer staff are paying a price the senior planners never had to pay, because the senior planners set the norms in the first place, and fit them without effort.

She is also aware that she cannot see the effort directly, and that her reading of who is braced could itself be wrong, which is why she plans to ask as well as watch.

steps.label: List the unwritten norms
steps.text:
She writes down the unwritten norms of her department as honestly as she can: suits for site meetings and most office days, a particular way of speaking in committee, a habit of small talk about holidays and house prices, a team social at a wine bar, an expectation that nobody leaves before the director. She asks two colleagues she trusts to add to the list. They add several she had not noticed, including a habit of mimicking accents in jokes.

She also notices that several norms on the list were never decided by anyone; they simply arrived with the people who were there first, and stayed.

She also notices that several norms on the list exist mainly because the department's founders were all from similar backgrounds, and that nobody has questioned them since.

steps.label: Mark what the work needs
steps.text:
For each norm, she asks whether the work genuinely requires it. Formal dress for public inquiries and committee meetings: yes. Suits on ordinary office days: no. A clear, precise style in written reports: yes. One particular accent in meetings: no. Leaving after the director: no. Jokes about accents: certainly not. She finds that most of the norms on the list are habit rather than need.

She also asks whether any of the necessary norms could be explained more clearly to newcomers, so that nobody has to guess them.

She also notices that "professionalism" has been used in two recent appraisals to criticise staff whose work was excellent, and rewrites the department's guidance to say what it means.

steps.label: Relax one norm at a time
steps.text:
She starts with dress, telling the team that ordinary smart clothes are fine on office days and that suits are needed only for committee and inquiries. She changes the team social from the wine bar to a rotating choice, including a café breakfast and a walk. She mentions in a team meeting that the accent jokes will stop, without naming anyone. She does not make speeches about diversity.

She also notices that two senior planners grumble about the dress change, and that both of them come in wearing more relaxed clothes within a month.

She also makes a point of not announcing the changes as being for anyone in particular, so that nobody feels singled out as the reason.

She also asks HR to check whether the department's dress guidance has ever been applied differently to different staff.

steps.label: Go first
steps.text:
She begins, in small ways, to share something of her own background: that she grew up on a farm in Lincolnshire, that her father left school at fourteen, that she still says "duck" to people when she is tired. Ruth, in the case at the start of this chapter, did the same. When the leader shows a less polished self, it becomes safer for others to do so.

She also notices that it is harder than she expected, and that she has been covering a little herself for thirty years.

She also notices that one senior planner, after hearing about the farm, mentions for the first time that he grew up above a chip shop, which surprises everyone.

She keeps it short and occasional. A leader who talks about herself constantly makes the room about her, which is a different problem.

steps.label: Watch without calling out
steps.text:
Over the following months, she notices that two of the newer staff have started to speak more in meetings, and that one comes to work in clothes that look like his own rather than a uniform. She says nothing about any of it. Remarking on a switch, even kindly, would expose the effort she is trying to reduce.

She also resists the urge to praise the change in anyone's manner, which would turn their easing into something she had noticed and was watching.

She also notices that Kwame laughs more freely in team meetings, and resists the temptation to mention it to him.

steps.label: Check what people actually feel
steps.text:
At the end of six months, she includes two questions in the team's anonymous survey: whether people feel they can be themselves at work, and what, if anything, makes that harder. The answers show improvement, and also name one thing she had not thought of: that team meetings are always at eight, which is hard for parents and for people who pray at dawn. She moves them to ten.

She also shares the results with the team, including the parts that are still not good enough, which earns her more trust than the improvements do.

She also asks the team which norms they would like to keep, and finds that several people value the formal committee style, which stays.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
A year later, none of the newer staff have left, which is a first for the department. Kwame tells her that he still switches at committee meetings, as everyone does, but that he no longer feels he has to be someone else at his desk. Bev keeps her list of norms and reviews it every year. She notices that the senior planners seem more relaxed too, and that the walks have become the most popular social.

She also passes the list to the other heads of department, without the names, and two of them begin the same exercise.

She also notices that she herself says "duck" more often, and that nobody minds.

moreFailures.title: Rewarding only one version
moreFailures.body:
In many workplaces, appraisals, promotions and informal praise reward a particular style: a neutral accent, a measured voice, contained gestures, polished small talk, certain clothes. People who already have that style are rewarded for being themselves; people who have to switch into it are rewarded for switching, and quietly penalised when they do not. McCluney and colleagues found that both Black and white evaluators rated a Black employee who code-switched as more professional than one who did not. The result is that switching becomes a condition of advancement, and its cost falls on the people who differ most from the norm. If you assess others, check your criteria for style that the work does not need, as the drill in this chapter suggests, and look for what people actually do. Polish is not the same as competence.

A useful check is to ask whether your highest performers all share one style, and whether the work explains that.

moreFailures.title: Demanding authenticity
moreFailures.body:
The opposite mistake is to urge people to drop their switch: "Just be yourself here," "You don't have to put on a voice for us," "We want the real you." It is meant kindly, and it puts the burden back on the person to take a risk that they, not you, will bear if it goes wrong. The previous chapter on masking described the same problem with unmasking. A man who switches at work has usually learned, from experience, what happens when he does not. Telling him that it is safe does not make it safe; changing the room does. The useful approach is the one Bev took: widen the norms, go first in showing a less polished self, stop the jokes and comments that make switching necessary, and then let people decide for themselves, in their own time, how much to change.

It also helps to remember that people may switch for reasons that have nothing to do with you, and are not yours to remove.

Notice, too, that "be yourself" is easiest to say for people who have never had to be anyone else.

moreFailures.title: Speaking for someone
moreFailures.body:
Some managers and colleagues, noticing that someone's natural style is read harshly by clients or senior staff, try to help by speaking for them: summarising their point in more polished language, explaining their manner to others, presenting their work for them. It can be well meant, and it can protect someone in a hostile room for a moment. But it tends to confirm the very reading it is meant to correct, by implying that the person cannot be understood without translation, and it takes visibility away from them. The chapter on the glass ceiling in Part IV described the difference between amplifying someone's point, which hands the floor back to them, and restating it in your own words. Hand the floor back. If a room is reading someone unfairly, challenge the room, not the person's style.

If you have to bridge a gap for a client, do it briefly and then turn to your colleague: "Kwame can take you through the detail."

moreFailures.title: Reading the switch as disloyalty
moreFailures.body:
The cost of switching is felt at home as well as at work. Family and old friends may read a man's work voice, clothes or manners as a sign that he has changed, looks down on them or has abandoned where he came from: "You've gone posh," "You sound like a white man," "Too good for us now." The chapter on class described Stephen, whose cousins teased him for exactly this. Such comments can make a man feel that he belongs fully in neither world, which is one of the identity costs this chapter describes. If someone you love switches for work, try not to read it as a verdict on you. Ask how it is for them, and let them be both people without having to choose. Both are real, as this chapter says; neither cancels the other.

If you are the one switching, it can help to tell family plainly that the work voice is for work, and that the home voice is still yours.

And notice whether the people who tease are themselves switching, in other places, without anyone remarking on it.

questions.a:
Not in itself. Adapting how you speak, dress and move to different settings is something almost everyone does, and Day and colleagues' 2002 meta-analysis found that high self-monitors, people who adapt readily, tended to receive better performance ratings and to emerge more often as leaders. The ability to read a room and fit it is a real skill. The problem this chapter describes is not switching but its cost when it is constant, unchosen and driven by fear of being judged or punished, especially when it falls most heavily on people whose natural style differs most from the norm. The difference between skill and survival lies in choice and cost: whether you switch because you want to, in a way you endorse, and whether you can drop it when you are somewhere safe.

It also helps to notice that most people switch in some way, which makes it easier to be generous about how others do it.

It also helps to remember that people switch in many directions, not only towards the norms of the powerful.

questions.q: How can I tell whether my own switching has become survival?
questions.a:
Look for the signs this chapter describes. You are exhausted in a way the work itself does not explain, as Marcus was on Friday nights. You are short-tempered at home after days of switching. You cannot drop the switch even with people you trust, as Connor could not at his sister's birthday. You feel a jolt of fear when someone sees the other version of you, as Marcus did at the team lunch. You no longer know which version is really you. The Switch Map and Release Points drills help you see where the cost falls. If several of these signs fit, it is worth looking for places where you can stop switching, and, if the exhaustion is affecting your health or relationships, talking to your GP or someone you trust.

It can also help to talk with others who switch in similar ways, who may recognise the cost and share what helps.

questions.q: Why does switching tire me out if I am good at it?
questions.a:
Because it takes effort to monitor yourself all day, even when you do it well. Hülsheger and Schewe combined ninety-five studies of emotional labour and found that surface acting, displaying what you do not feel, was strongly linked to exhaustion, while deep acting, actually feeling what you display, was much less so. Switching often involves a great deal of surface acting: the laugh at the joke that is not funny, the neutral face over an irritation, the careful voice over your natural one. A popular explanation for this kind of fatigue, that willpower is a limited tank that runs out, has not held up in large replications. The more likely explanation is the ongoing effort of monitoring and the strain of hiding parts of yourself, which is why places and people where you can stop matter so much.

It also helps to build in time with people who know all of you, which is where the monitoring can finally stop.

It also helps to know that surface acting is the costly part, so finding something you genuinely feel, even appreciation, can ease the load.

questions.q: What can a manager do about code-switching in a team?
questions.a:
Look at the room rather than the people. List the unwritten norms of dress, speech, socialising and behaviour in your team, and ask which ones the work genuinely needs, as Bev did. Relax the ones it does not. Stop jokes about accents, hair, food and backgrounds, and do not mimic how anyone speaks. Assess people on what they do, not on polish. Go first in showing a less guarded self, as Ruth and Bev both did. Do not call out anyone's switch, and do not urge people to drop it; change the conditions that make it necessary and let them decide. Ask, anonymously, whether people feel they can be themselves at work and what makes it harder, and act on the answers. The aim is not to stop switching but to make it a choice rather than a toll.

It also helps to accept that some switching will remain, because some settings do have genuine requirements, and to be clear about which ones.

It also helps to notice who in the team has never had to switch, since they may be the last to see the problem.

questions.q: My partner seems like a different person at work events. Should I say something?
questions.a:
Not in front of others, and not as a criticism. If your partner switches at work events, they may be doing what many people do, adapting to a setting with its own expectations, or they may be working hard to be accepted in a setting where their natural style is judged. Either way, pointing it out in public, as Marcus's colleague did at the team lunch, exposes something they may be working to keep invisible. In private, and with curiosity rather than judgment, you might ask how those events feel for them, and whether there is anything that would make them easier. Then listen. It may help them to know that you see both versions and love both, and that with you they do not need to switch at all.

If your partner tells you it is hard, take it seriously, and consider whether you can make those events easier, for example by staying close or leaving early together.

And notice which version of yourself your partner sees most, and whether they would like to see the other one more often.

questions.q: How can I adapt to another culture without losing myself?
questions.a:
Molinsky's work suggests looking at two separate difficulties: competence, learning how the new behaviour is done, and identity, deciding whether and how far you are willing to do it. For competence, watch people you admire in the new setting, ask colleagues to explain the unwritten rules and practise in low-stakes moments. For identity, look for a version of the new behaviour that you can endorse, as Piotr did: he learned to describe his own contribution plainly while still crediting his team first, which felt honest to him. You do not have to choose between adopting the new culture completely and refusing it. Many people find a blend that works, and keep places, people and habits from their first culture where they can be fully themselves.

It also helps to stay in touch with people from your first culture, who can remind you who you were before you started adapting.

It also helps to forgive yourself the awkward early attempts, which almost everyone makes when they first adapt to a new setting.

watch.title: Jamila Lyiscott: 3 ways to speak English
watch.notice: A spoken-word piece about moving between three ways of speaking English. Watch how her voice, rhythm and body change with each, and how she refuses to rank them.

watch.title: Uncovering Talent: The Power of Authenticity
watch.notice: Kenji Yoshino on covering: playing down an identity so that others are comfortable. Listen for the four ways people cover, and notice which you recognise.

watch.title: Sorry to Bother You: The Art of the White Voice
watch.notice: A satire in which a Black telemarketer succeeds only when he adopts a white voice. Notice how much of the switch the film locates in the voice, and what it implies about who sets the norm.

watch.title: Blindspotting: Official Trailer
watch.notice: Two friends in a changing Oakland, one Black and on probation, one white. Notice how differently each man's body and manner are read, and how carefully one of them has to move.

reviewPrompt: This week, notice one switch you make and what it costs, and never remark aloud on someone else's.
